_note: Ballpark per-second USD rates used for the UI's cost ESTIMATES only — nothing here is billed. Verified against fal.ai's model pages (July 2026) and segmind.com's (August 2026); edit freely when a vendor's prices move. Every figure the UI shows from these is labeled 'estimate'.

kling._source: fal.ai kling-video o3 STANDARD reference-to-video (July 2026): $0.112/s with audio, $0.084/s audio off — flat across durations, ~720p output (pro: 1080p at $0.14/s). Approve's Topaz upscale lifts the master to 1080p. Probe rides the same endpoint.

seedance._source: fal.ai bytedance/seedance-2.0/reference-to-video standard tier (July 2026): $0.014 per 1000 tokens for 480p/720p/1080p ($0.008/1k for 4k); tokens = height*width*seconds*24/1024 — so 720p=$0.3024/s, 1080p=$0.6804/s (fal quotes $0.682). Probe = SAME standard endpoint at probeResolution; the mini/fast tiers are deliberately not used (character fidelity drift).

seedance-2.5@fal._source: fal bytedance/seedance-2.5/reference-to-video (August 2026): $0.0214 per 1000 tokens; tokens = height*width*(input+output seconds)*24/1024 — so 16:9 output alone is $0.2205/s at 480p and $0.4730/s at 720p (16:9-derived, the same convention as the Seedance 2.0 row; other ratios differ slightly). Image and audio references are free; VIDEO references bill their input seconds at a 0.6 multiplier, which this estimate does not model. 2.5 is materially dearer than 2.0 — it must never share that row.

topaz._source: fal.ai/models/fal-ai/topaz/upscale/video (checked 2026-08-13). fal DOCUMENTS three per-second tiers by OUTPUT resolution — up to 720p $0.01/s, 720p–1080p $0.02/s, ABOVE 1080p $0.08/s — plus 'price doubles for 60fps output' and 'for Gaia 2 output costs half of the prices'. It does NOT document how the tier is measured, and that is the whole difficulty. REAL INVOICE: a user upscaling a 15s 480p 9:16 clip to 1080p was charged ~$1.28 — that is the $0.08/s ABOVE-1080p tier (15s × $0.08 = $1.20; the extra ~$0.08 is one second of fal's own billing granularity, which this estimate does not model), NOT the $0.02/s tier the '480p → 1080p' reading predicts ($0.30). INFERENCE (not documented, from that one invoice): fal tiers on the output frame's HEIGHT. This app defaults to 9:16 and upscalePlan lifts the SHORT side to 1080, so a 480×854 portrait source comes back 1080×1920 — 1920 pixels tall, which fal bills as above-1080p. Height is the only rule that fits BOTH the invoice and fal's own tier names: a long-side or pixel-count rule would put landscape 1920×1080 (the canonical '1080p') in the top tier too, and then the documented middle tier could never apply to anything. Landscape and square outputs therefore quote by their real height (1920×1080 → $0.02/s), which is what the docs say and what nothing contradicts. AMBIGUOUS CASES ROUND UP, DELIBERATELY: unknown source dimensions (nothing rendered yet, no recorded short side, or no aspect) fall to defaultResolution — the DEAREST tier — because the app's own default is the portrait shape that bills there, and a surprise bill on a paid button costs trust in a way a cautious quote does not. 60fps is NOT modelled: the fal path sends only {video_url, upscale_factor, model} (src/lib/fal.js topazArgs) and never asks for 60fps output, so the doubling cannot apply here — target_fps pinning is the SEGMIND path, and Segmind bills flat anyway. gaia2Multiplier applies only when FAL_TOPAZ_MODEL names Gaia 2 unambiguously; a bare 'Gaia' pays full, since halving on a guess is the under-quote this row exists to prevent. REPLACES a flat $0.12/s ballpark that quoted $1.80 for the invoice above. If real invoices ever contradict the height rule, correct tierMaxOutputHeight here — the estimator reads the ladder from this row and states nothing of its own.

seedance-2.0@segmind._source: segmind.com/models/seedance-2.0/pricing (checked 2026-08-10), 16:9 column — the same 16:9-derived convention as the fal Seedance rows. 9:16 is identical to 16:9; the other ratios differ by under 2% at the low tiers (1:1 $0.0672/$0.1512, 4:3 and 3:4 $0.0691/$0.1522, 21:9 $0.0703/$0.1519) and 1080p/4k are flat across every ratio. Segmind is roughly HALF fal's rate for the SAME model (fal 2.0: $0.135/$0.3024) — that gap is real and re-checkable, not a transcription slip, so please verify against the page before 'fixing' it.

seedance-2.5@segmind._source: segmind.com/models/seedance-2.5/pricing (checked 2026-08-10), 16:9 column. Segmind publishes NO 1080p and NO 4k tier for 2.5 — these two rates are the whole table, so a spec pinning a higher resolution fails loudly here rather than quoting a tier that does not exist (seedance-2.5@fal behaves the same way). 9:16 matches 16:9; other ratios differ by under 3% (1:1 $0.1018/$0.2389, 4:3 and 3:4 $0.1046/$0.2404, 21:9 $0.1065/$0.2401). Turning audio generation on does NOT change the price. Requests carrying VIDEO references bill a ~40%-cheaper video-to-video tier ($0.0637/s at 480p, $0.1429/s at 720p), which this estimate does not model — the same unmodelled discount the fal 2.5 row carries. Segmind is roughly HALF fal's rate for the SAME model (fal 2.5: $0.2205/$0.4730) — verified, not a typo.

topaz@segmind._source: segmind.com/models/topaz-video-upscale/pricing (checked 2026-08-10): $0.125 per second, FLAT, billed on the INPUT video's duration — which is exactly what estimateUpscale sums (one Topaz job per sub-HD clip). The page publishes this single rate and NO per-target-resolution breakdown, so 720p/1080p/4k targets are deliberately not priced differently here; a per-resolution map would be invented, not sourced. UPSCALE_TARGET_RESOLUTION therefore changes what you get, not what this estimate says.

_unpriced: Rows shaped {"perSecondUsd": null} are a KNOWN UNKNOWN, not a free tier and not a typo: the model renders, it bills, and the vendor simply does not publish a per-second rate. The estimator answers totalUsd:null + an unknownPrice hint for these instead of throwing or borrowing a sibling's rate — an invented figure on a paid button is worse than no figure. Each row is INDEPENDENT (never an $alias of another): filling one in must never silently price the others. NO SHIPPED VENDOR ROW IS CURRENTLY UNPRICED — Segmind's three rates landed 2026-08-10. The path is still live and still correct for the next vendor that publishes nothing, so the synthetic rows below keep it exercised; see _fixtures.
_fixtures: SYNTHETIC rows for a vendor that does not exist. They exist so the unknown-price path (estimator's null branch, the UI's amber "Price not set" note, the ledger's unpriced flag) stays covered WITHOUT depending on a real vendor staying unpriced — the last time that coupling existed, pricing Segmind broke seven test files. Never point a registry backend at 'examplevendor', and never delete these to 'clean up': the coverage goes with them. Marked _fixture so the no-_todo guard in estimator-providers.test.js can tell 'unpriced on purpose, forever' from 'shipped before anyone looked the rate up'.

seedance-2.0@examplevendor._fixture: Synthetic. Drives estimateRender's unpriced branch. See _fixtures.

topaz@examplevendor._fixture: Synthetic. Drives estimateUpscale's unpriced branch, and its _todo below keeps the 'where to look it up' half of the hint covered. See _fixtures.

_aliases: Rows shaped {"$alias": "<key>"} are ONE-HOP redirects, not rate tables. The CLI records the CANONICAL compound backend id (<model>@<provider>) in render.json, and the estimate endpoint prices CLI-created runs off that value — these hops send it to the legacy rate row above instead of throwing. Only ONE hop is followed, so a genuinely unknown id (kling-o3@segmind) still fails loudly.
